mainEntity.name: How long do flexible dentures typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flexible dentures generally have an expected lifespan of around five to eight years, though this varies depending on the quality of fit, how well they are maintained, and how much the underlying bone and gum tissue changes over time. Regular professional reviews can help identify when a denture is approaching the end of its useful life and whether adjustment, relining, or replacement is the most appropriate course of action. Individual outcomes will depend on clinical factors assessed by your dentist.

mainEntity.name: Can I adjust my flexible denture myself at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is strongly advisable not to attempt adjusting a flexible denture at home. The nylon thermoplastic material requires specific professional tools and expertise to modify safely. DIY adjustments can permanently damage the denture, alter the fit unpredictably, and may create sharp surfaces that cause soft tissue injury. If your denture is causing discomfort or feels loose, contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment. Early professional intervention is generally much simpler than addressing problems that have been worsened by home modification attempts.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for flexible dentures to feel loose after a few years?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is quite normal for a degree of loosening to occur over time. This is primarily due to the gradual resorption of the jawbone that follows tooth loss — a natural biological process rather than a fault with the denture itself. As the bone ridge changes shape, a denture that once fitted precisely will begin to feel less stable. This does not mean the denture cannot be improved; relining, adjusting, or replacing the appliance are all options your dentist can discuss with you following an assessment.

mainEntity.name: Are flexible dentures suitable for everyone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flexible dentures are not universally suitable for all patients or all clinical situations. They are typically most appropriate as partial dentures rather than full dentures, and their suitability depends on a range of clinical factors including the number and distribution of missing teeth, the health and quality of the remaining natural teeth, the condition of the gum tissue and supporting bone, and the patient's overall oral health. A thorough clinical examination is necessary before recommending flexible dentures, and your dentist will discuss all available options with you so that you can make an informed decision.

mainEntity.name: Can gum disease affect the fit of my flexible denture?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Gum disease — whether affecting the tissue around remaining natural teeth or the gum ridge beneath a denture — can cause changes in the shape, volume, and health of the soft tissues that support the appliance. Swelling associated with active gum inflammation may temporarily make a denture feel tighter, whilst recession or tissue loss can cause loosening. Managing gum health is therefore an important aspect of maintaining a comfortable denture fit. If you are concerned about your gum health, your dental team can provide assessment and appropriate guidance for gum disease.

mainEntity.name: What is denture-related stomatitis and how can it be managed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture-related stomatitis is a common condition in which the gum tissue covered by a denture becomes red and inflamed. It is often associated with the presence of Candida albicans (a type of fungus) and is more likely to develop when a denture is worn continuously without adequate cleaning. Management typically involves improved denture hygiene, ensuring the denture is removed at night, antifungal treatment where appropriate, and addressing any fit issues that may be contributing. Your dentist can assess and advise on the most suitable management approach for your individual situation.
